blocks.body:
If you add a set of $k$ integers to itself, how many different sums can you get? At most $k(k+1)/2$, when all sums are distinct, and at least $2k-1$. The lower bound is attained only by arithmetic progressions. So the size of $A+A$ already says something about the shape of $A$. Additive combinatorics turns that observation into a theory. Sets with few sums are forced to look like progressions (Freiman's theorem), and Fourier analysis on $\mathbb Z/N$ measures how far a set is from random.

The payoff is a set of tools strong enough to find patterns in sets about which you know almost nothing except their size. This is how Roth proved that dense sets contain three-term progressions, and it is one of the ingredients in Green and Tao's theorem that the primes contain arbitrarily long ones.

blocks.title: Sumset and doubling constant
blocks.body:
For finite subsets $A,B$ of an abelian group (here $\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb Z/N$),
$$A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\},\qquad A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.$$
The doubling constant of $A$ is $K=|A+A|/|A|$. The set $A$ has small doubling if $|A+A|\le K|A|$ for a $K$ that stays bounded as $|A|$ grows.

Small doubling means that many of the $|A|^2$ pairs collide on the same sum, which is a strong form of additive structure.

blocks.title: Three test cases
blocks.body:
Compare three sets of size $k$.

- An arithmetic progression $\{a,a+d,\dots,a+(k-1)d\}$: the sums are $2a+jd$ for $0\le j\le2k-2$, so $|A+A|=2k-1$ and $K\lt 2$.
- Powers of two $\{1,2,4,\dots,2^{k-1}\}$: by uniqueness of binary expansions, $2^i+2^j$ with $i\le j$ are all different, so $|A+A|=k(k+1)/2$, the maximum.
- Two far-apart blocks $\{1,\dots,k\}\cup\{10^6+1,\dots,10^6+k\}$ (size $2k$, with $k$ small compared with $10^6$): the sums fill three blocks of length $2k-1$, so $|A+A|=3(2k-1)$ and $K\approx3$. This set is not a progression, but it is a two-dimensional progression $\{x+10^6y:1\le x\le k,\ 0\le y\le1\}$.

The third example is the general picture. Small doubling does not force a progression, but it does force a set to sit efficiently inside a "progression of bounded dimension".

blocks.title: Sumsets in the integers
blocks.body: For a finite set $A\subset\mathbb Z$ with $|A|=k\ge1$ we have $|A+A|\ge2k-1$, with equality if and only if $A$ is an arithmetic progression.

Write $A=\{a_1\lt a_2\lt \dots\lt a_k\}$. The $2k-1$ sums
$$a_1+a_1\lt a_1+a_2\lt a_2+a_2\lt a_2+a_3\lt a_3+a_3\lt \dots\lt a_{k-1}+a_k\lt a_k+a_k$$
are strictly increasing, hence distinct, so $|A+A|\ge2k-1$.

Suppose equality holds, so this chain is all of $A+A$. For $2\le i\le k-1$ the sum $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$ lies strictly between $a_{i-1}+a_i$ and $a_i+a_{i+1}$. In the chain the only element strictly between those two is $a_i+a_i$. Hence $a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}=2a_i$ for every such $i$, which says $A$ is an arithmetic progression. Conversely a progression has exactly $2k-1$ sums.

blocks.title: Cauchy–Davenport theorem
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be prime and $A,B$ nonempty subsets of $\mathbb Z/p$. Then
$$|A+B|\ge\min\bigl(p,\ |A|+|B|-1\bigr).$$

blocks.title: Proof (Davenport's transform)
blocks.body:
We use induction on $|B|$. If $|B|=1$ then $|A+B|=|A|$ and the claim holds. Let $|B|\ge2$ and assume the result for all smaller second sets. If $A+B=\mathbb Z/p$ there is nothing to prove, so assume not.

For $e\in\mathbb Z/p$ define
$$A'=A\cup(B+e),\qquad B'=B\cap(A-e).$$
Two facts hold for every $e$.

1. $A'+B'\subseteq A+B$. Take $y\in B'$, so $y\in B$ and $y+e\in A$. If $x\in A$ then $x+y\in A+B$. If $x=b+e$ with $b\in B$ then $x+y=b+(y+e)\in B+A$.
2. $|A'|+|B'|=|A|+|B|$. Indeed $|A'|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap(B+e)|$, and $|B'|=|(B+e)\cap A|$ after translating by $e$.

We now choose $e$ so that $B'$ is nonempty and smaller than $B$. For any $e=a-b$ with $a\in A$, $b\in B$, we have $b\in B'$, so $B'\neq\varnothing$. Suppose that for every such $e$ we had $B'=B$, that is, $B+e\subseteq A$. Fix distinct $b,b'\in B$ and put $d=b'-b\neq0$. For each $a\in A$, taking $e=a-b$ gives $a+d=b'+e\in A$. So $A+d\subseteq A$, hence $A+d=A$, and $A$ is a union of cosets of the subgroup generated by $d$. That subgroup is all of $\mathbb Z/p$ because $p$ is prime. Then $A=\mathbb Z/p$ and $A+B=\mathbb Z/p$, contrary to assumption.

So some $e$ gives $1\le|B'|\lt |B|$. By the induction hypothesis and facts 1 and 2,
$$|A+B|\ge|A'+B'|\ge\min(p,\ |A'|+|B'|-1)=\min(p,\ |A|+|B|-1).$$

blocks.title: Two quick consequences
blocks.body:
(a) Show that if $A,B\subseteq\mathbb Z/n$ satisfy $|A|+|B|>n$, then $A+B=\mathbb Z/n$. Deduce that every residue modulo an odd prime $p$ is a sum of two squares.

(b) Let $p\equiv1\pmod3$ be prime. Show that every residue mod $p$ is a sum of three cubes mod $p$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Fix $g\in\mathbb Z/n$. The sets $A$ and $g-B=\{g-b:b\in B\}$ have sizes adding to more than $n$, so they intersect: some $a=g-b$, that is, $g=a+b$. (No primality is needed.) For the squares, let $S=\{x^2:x\in\mathbb Z/p\}$. The nonzero squares come in pairs $x^2=(-x)^2$, so there are $(p-1)/2$ of them (see [[quadratic-residues]]), and $|S|=(p+1)/2$. Then $|S|+|S|=p+1>p$, so $S+S=\mathbb Z/p$.

(b) Here pigeonhole is not enough, and Cauchy–Davenport does the work. Since $3\mid p-1$, the map $x\mapsto x^3$ on $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ has a kernel of size $3$ (the cube roots of unity), so it is $3$-to-$1$, and there are $(p-1)/3$ nonzero cubes. With $0$, the set $C$ of cubes has $|C|=(p+2)/3$, and $|C|+|C|=(2p+4)/3\lt p$ for every such $p$ (all are at least $7$). Applying Cauchy–Davenport twice,
$$|C+C+C|\ge\min\bigl(p,\ |C+C|+|C|-1\bigr)\ge\min\bigl(p,\ 3|C|-2\bigr)=\min(p,\ p)=p.$$
(If the first application already gives $C+C=\mathbb Z/p$, the conclusion is immediate.) So $C+C+C=\mathbb Z/p$. Two cubes are not always enough: mod $7$ the cubes are $\{0,1,6\}$ and $C+C=\{0,1,2,5,6\}$ misses $3$ and $4$.

blocks.title: Ruzsa's triangle inequality
blocks.body:
For finite subsets $A,B,C$ of an abelian group,
$$|A|\,|B-C|\le|A-B|\,|A-C|.$$

For each $x\in B-C$ fix one representation $x=b(x)-c(x)$ with $b(x)\in B$, $c(x)\in C$. Define
$$\phi:A\times(B-C)\to(A-B)\times(A-C),\qquad\phi(a,x)=\bigl(a-b(x),\ a-c(x)\bigr).$$
If $\phi(a,x)=(u,v)$ then $v-u=b(x)-c(x)=x$, so $x$ is determined. Then $b(x)$ is determined, and $a=u+b(x)$. So $\phi$ is injective, and comparing sizes gives the inequality.

blocks.title: Structure: Plünnecke–Ruzsa and Freiman
blocks.body:
Small doubling propagates. The Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality says that if $|A+A|\le K|A|$ then
$$|mA-nA|\le K^{m+n}|A|\qquad\text{for all }m,n\ge0,$$
where $mA$ means $A+\dots+A$ with $m$ summands. (Petridis found a one-page proof in 2012; we omit it.) Ruzsa's triangle inequality gives a weaker version immediately: with $(A,B,C)$ replaced by $(-A,A,A)$ it reads $|A|\,|A-A|\le|A+A|^2$, so $|A-A|\le K^2|A|$.

A generalised arithmetic progression of dimension $d$ is a set
$$P=\{a_0+n_1d_1+\dots+n_dd_d:\ 0\le n_i\lt L_i\},$$
of size at most $L_1\cdots L_d$. It always has small doubling: $P+P$ is contained in a progression of the same shape with each $L_i$ doubled, so $|P+P|\le2^dL_1\cdots L_d$. Freiman's theorem is the converse.

Freiman's theorem: if $A\subset\mathbb Z$ is finite and $|A+A|\le K|A|$, then $A$ is contained in a generalised arithmetic progression of dimension at most $d(K)$ and size at most $f(K)\,|A|$, where $d(K)$ and $f(K)$ depend only on $K$.

Ruzsa (1994) found a short proof combining the inequalities above with a covering argument, and Chang and Sanders later made the dependence on $K$ far better. In the group $\mathbb F_2^n$ the natural analogue, Marton's polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa conjecture, was proved by Gowers, Green, Manners and Tao in 2023: such a set is covered by a number of cosets of a subgroup of size at most $|A|$, where that number is polynomial in $K$.

blocks.title: Fourier analysis on Z/N
blocks.body:
Write $e(t)=e^{2\pi it}$ and, for $A\subseteq\mathbb Z/N$, define $S_A(r)=\sum_{a\in A}e(ra/N)$. Then $S_A(0)=|A|$, and orthogonality of characters (see [[fourier-poisson]]) gives Parseval's identity $\sum_r|S_A(r)|^2=N|A|$. Additive questions become questions about these sums, because $\frac1N\sum_re(rm/N)$ is $1$ if $m\equiv0$ and $0$ otherwise.

- Additive energy. $$E(A)=\#\{(a,b,c,d)\in A^4:a+b=c+d\}=\frac1N\sum_r|S_A(r)|^4$$.
- Three-term progressions. $$T(A)=\#\{(x,y,z)\in A^3:x+z=2y\}=\frac1N\sum_rS_A(r)^2S_A(-2r)$$.

In the last formula the term $r=0$ is $|A|^3/N$, the count expected for a random set of the same density. Everything else is controlled by the largest nontrivial coefficient. Indeed, for $N$ odd, $r\mapsto-2r$ is a bijection, so
$$\Bigl|T(A)-\frac{|A|^3}N\Bigr|\le\max_{r\neq0}|S_A(r)|\cdot\frac1N\sum_r|S_A(r)|^2=|A|\max_{r\ne0}|S_A(r)|.$$
So either $A$ has about the expected number of progressions, or some $|S_A(r)|$ is large, meaning $A$ is biased along the residues of $rx$. Roth's proof plays these two cases against each other (see [[arithmetic-progressions]]).

blocks.title: Energy bound
blocks.body: For a finite set $A$ in an abelian group, $|A+A|\ge|A|^4/E(A)$.

Let $\rho(x)$ be the number of pairs $(a,b)\in A^2$ with $a+b=x$. Then $\sum_x\rho(x)=|A|^2$, $\sum_x\rho(x)^2=E(A)$, and $\rho$ vanishes outside $A+A$. By Cauchy–Schwarz,
$$|A|^4=\Bigl(\sum_{x\in A+A}\rho(x)\Bigr)^2\le|A+A|\sum_x\rho(x)^2=|A+A|\,E(A).$$

blocks.title: Quadratic residues look random
blocks.body: Let $p=101$ and let $Q$ be the $50$ nonzero squares mod $p$. Show that $|S_Q(r)|\le(1+\sqrt{101})/2\approx5.52$ for $r\neq0$. Use this to estimate the number $T(Q)$ of triples $(x,y,z)\in Q^3$ with $x+z\equiv2y$, and compare with the true value $1250$.
blocks.solution:
Using the Legendre symbol, the indicator of $Q$ on nonzero $x$ is $\tfrac12\bigl(1+\bigl(\tfrac xp\bigr)\bigr)$. So for $r\neq0$
$$S_Q(r)=\frac12\sum_{x\neq0}e(rx/p)+\frac12\sum_{x}\Bigl(\frac xp\Bigr)e(rx/p)=\frac12\Bigl(-1+\Bigl(\frac rp\Bigr)g\Bigr),$$
where $g=\sum_x\bigl(\frac xp\bigr)e(x/p)$ is the quadratic Gauss sum. Since $101\equiv1\pmod4$, $g=\sqrt{101}$ (see [[gauss-sums]]). So $S_Q(r)=(-1\pm\sqrt{101})/2$ and $|S_Q(r)|\le(1+\sqrt{101})/2\approx5.52$, compared with the trivial bound $50$.

The main term is $50^3/101\approx1237.6$, and the error is at most $50\times5.52\approx276$. So the bound predicts $T(Q)$ between about $961$ and $1514$. The true value is $1250$ (this includes the $50$ trivial triples $x=y=z$). The squares behave, for three-term progressions, like a random set of density $1/2$.

blocks.body:
- Cauchy–Davenport is false for composite moduli. In $\mathbb Z/6$, $A=B=\{0,2,4\}$ gives $|A+B|=3\lt \min(6,5)$. The obstruction is a subgroup, and Kneser's theorem says subgroups are the only obstruction in general abelian groups.
- Freiman's theorem says $A$ is contained in a generalised progression of comparable size. It does not say $A$ is one, nor that $A$ is a dense subset of an ordinary progression. The dimension must be allowed to grow with $K$. The standard example is a cube: the $2^d$ sums of distinct elements of $\{1,10,\dots,10^{d-1}\}$ have $|A+A|=3^d$, so doubling $(3/2)^d$.
- $|A+A|$ and $|A-A|$ can differ a lot for the same set, although each is at most the square of the other's doubling constant times $|A|$, by Ruzsa's inequality.
- Small Fourier coefficients control three-term progressions but not four-term ones. A set can have all $|S_A(r)|$ small and still have the wrong number of four-term progressions, for example a set defined by a condition on $x^2 \bmod N$. Longer progressions need Gowers's higher-order uniformity norms.

Fourier analysis and the density-increment strategy prove Roth's theorem and, with Gowers's higher-order Fourier analysis and Szemerédi's combinatorics, give the theory of [[arithmetic-progressions]]. Sets of minimal energy are [[sidon-sets]], and sets $A$ with $A+A$ (or $hA$) covering everything are [[additive-bases]]. The exponential sums $S_A(r)$ are the finite cousins of the sums in [[exponential-sums]] and the [[circle-method]], and colouring versions of these questions belong to [[ramsey-arithmetic]]. The elementary moves come from [[combinatorial-nt]].

On 8 October 2026 Thomas Bloom (erdosproblems.com) listed the claims touching Erdős problems in an OpenAI release. They include Erdős problem #3, claimed (not yet established) via a 198-page quasipolynomial bound for Szemerédi's theorem whose Lean file proves only a weaker statement. Bloom called his list a summary of claims, not an endorsement.

1. Show that $|A+B|\ge|A|+|B|-1$ for finite nonempty $A,B\subset\mathbb Z$. When does equality hold?
2. Use Ruzsa's triangle inequality to prove $|A-A|\le|A+A|^2/|A|$ and $|A+A|\le|A-A|^2/|A|$.
3. Compute the additive energy $E(A)$ for $A=\{1,2,\dots,k\}$ and compare $|A|^4/E(A)$ with $|A+A|$.
4. Let $A\subseteq\mathbb Z/p$ with $|A|=k$. Prove that $|hA|\ge\min(p,\ hk-h+1)$, where $hA$ is the $h$-fold sumset.
